Varicocelectomy-related orchialgia

One randomized trial of 60 men found lower 0-10 pain VAS after red or near-infrared laser than sham at 6 and 12 weeks. Reported sexual-satisfaction values declined without stated scale anchors, so their direction is unclear.

Publications and records

1unique publication and cohort

Publication and study types

Human RCT: 1 (n=60)

The post-varicocelectomy cohort is also cross-listed in the Testicular pain row; it is counted once as a cohort.

Clinical effect sizes (estimate)

Pain VAS (0-10), mean +/- SD; active vs sham: red, 3.6 +/- 0.8 vs 4.4 +/- 0.6 at week 6 and 2.1 +/- 0.4 vs 3.3 +/- 1.4 at week 12; near-infrared, 3.7 +/- 0.3 vs 4.4 +/- 0.6 at week 6 and 2.1 +/- 1.0 vs 3.3 +/- 1.4 at week 12. Active-versus-sham p=.0001 for both groups at week 6; p=.001 for red and p=.003 for near-infrared at week 12.

Sexual-satisfaction VAS (0-10; anchors not reported), baseline/week 6/week 12: red 8.2/3.8/2.0; near-infrared 8.0/4.0/1.1; sham 8.9/5.4/4.0. Values decline although the authors describe improvement, so the direction is unclear (Momenzadeh et al., 2024).

Certainty of evidence (estimate)

Low for short-term pain reduction; very low for sexual-satisfaction outcomes (reported VAS direction unclear)

PBM Database summary

What the records report

One randomized trial of 60 men found lower 0-10 pain VAS after red or near-infrared laser than sham at 6 and 12 weeks. Reported sexual-satisfaction values declined without stated scale anchors, so their direction is unclear.

Summary of the Evidence

One 60-participant randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled trial examined persistent orchialgia after varicocelectomy. It randomized 20 men each to red laser, near-infrared laser, or sham. This cohort is distinct from the chronic testicular-pain trial in the preceding indication row, although the post-varicocelectomy paper is cross-listed there; it is not a second cohort.

Human and clinical evidence

At 6 and 12 weeks, both active-light groups had lower pain VAS values than sham. The paper also says sexual satisfaction improved, but the reported 0-10 values fell in every group and score anchors were not defined, so the direction cannot be interpreted reliably (Momenzadeh et al., 2024).

Animal evidence

No animal model directly examining pain after varicocelectomy was identified; testicular-injury animal studies were not treated as postoperative-pain evidence.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No separate cell, tissue or ex-vivo study directly examined post-varicocelectomy orchialgia.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The trial compared 650-nm red light at 50 mW and 820-nm near-infrared light at 100 mW with sham. A contact probe was applied bilaterally near the upper scrotal nerve for 15 minutes, three times weekly over 12 sessions. The authors report a fluence of 6-25 J/cm2/day. Since wavelength and power varied together, the trial does not establish a preferred wavelength or dose.

Interpretation

The single small trial supports a short-term pain effect through 12 weeks, but independent replication, longer follow-up, and evidence about function, recurrence, and adverse effects are lacking. Sexual-satisfaction change remains uncertain because published score values fall without stated anchors.

Rationale for the certainty assessment

One 60-participant sham-controlled trial found lower pain VAS in both active groups than sham at 6 and 12 weeks. The study supports a short-term postoperative-pain signal, but it is a single small trial from one research group with no follow-up beyond 12 weeks. Sexual-satisfaction means fell in all arms despite the authors' stated improvement, and the scale anchors are unstated, so that outcome cannot be interpreted confidently.
